facts.title: Named After Stone
facts.text: Lithium was discovered in 1817 by Swedish chemist Johan August Arfwedson while analyzing the mineral petalite. Its name comes from the Greek word 'lithos', meaning stone, because it was first found in minerals rather than in plant tissue or animal blood like the other alkali metals sodium and potassium known at the time. The pure metal was not isolated until 1821, when William Thomas Brande and Humphry Davy obtained it by electrolysis of lithium oxide.

facts.title: The Lightest Metal
facts.text: Lithium is the lightest of all metals and the least dense solid element at room temperature, with a density of about 0.534 grams per cubic centimetre. That is only about half the density of water, so a chunk of lithium would float, if it did not react violently with the water at the same time. It is soft enough to be cut with a kitchen knife and reveals a bright silvery surface that quickly tarnishes in air.

facts.title: Born In The Big Bang
facts.text: Lithium is one of only three elements, along with hydrogen and helium, created in the first few minutes after the Big Bang through Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Curiously, astronomers observe far less lithium in old stars than the theory predicts, a long-standing puzzle known as the 'cosmological lithium problem'. Stars also tend to destroy lithium in their hot interiors, which is why finding it in a star's atmosphere tells astronomers something about that star's age and structure.

facts.title: Medicine For The Mind
facts.text: Lithium salts, especially lithium carbonate, are a frontline treatment for bipolar disorder and were pioneered by Australian psychiatrist John Cade in 1949. It is one of the simplest drugs in all of medicine, just a single charged atom, yet it remains one of the most effective mood stabilizers known and can reduce the risk of suicide in patients. Exactly how it works in the brain is still not fully understood, which makes it a fascinating subject of ongoing research.

facts.title: Powering The Modern World
facts.text: Lithium-ion batteries store energy in smartphones, laptops, and electric cars because lithium's tiny, light ions move easily and pack a lot of energy for their weight. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino for developing these batteries. John Goodenough was 97 when he received it, making him the oldest Nobel laureate in history at the time.

facts.title: Crimson Fingerprint In Flame
facts.text: When a lithium compound is held in a flame, it burns a vivid crimson-red, a signature used in chemistry classrooms for the 'flame test' to identify elements. This same effect gives certain red fireworks and signal flares their deep scarlet colour. The colour arises because heated lithium atoms emit light at very specific wavelengths, a quantum fingerprint unique to the element.

facts.title: Locked In Brine And Rock
facts.text: Most of the world's lithium is extracted either from hard-rock spodumene mines, notably in Australia, or by evaporating salty groundwater from desert basins. The 'Lithium Triangle' spanning Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile holds a huge share of global reserves in high-altitude salt flats like Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni. There, brine is pumped into vast ponds and left to evaporate in the sun for many months before the lithium is purified.

facts.title: Fuel For Fusion
facts.text: The lithium isotope lithium-6 is critical to thermonuclear weapons and to future fusion reactors because it can be bombarded with neutrons to breed tritium, a heavy form of hydrogen used as fusion fuel. Experimental fusion projects like ITER plan to line their reactor walls with lithium-containing 'blankets' to generate their own tritium supply. This makes a soft, lightweight metal a surprising key to the energy of the stars.

facts.title: A Greasy Second Job
facts.text: Beyond batteries and medicine, lithium has long been used to make lithium grease, a thick lubricant that stays stable across a wide range of temperatures and resists water. This is why many car wheel bearings and industrial machines rely on it. Lithium compounds are also added to glass and ceramics to make them more heat-resistant, and to special glass-ceramic cooktops and telescope mirrors that barely expand when heated.

facts.title: Reactive But Restrained
facts.text: As an alkali metal, lithium reacts with water to release hydrogen gas, but it does so far more gently than its cousins sodium and potassium, fizzing rather than exploding. It is so chemically eager that it must be stored under oil or in an inert atmosphere to keep it from reacting with moisture and nitrogen in the air. Remarkably, lithium is one of the very few elements that reacts directly with nitrogen gas at room temperature to form lithium nitride.
